Hiding the link is presentation, not protection — the route guard and, above all, the backend decide who may upload. What it buys is that the three roles who cannot upload are not shown a door that opens onto a 403.

One badge, not a list: a demo user holds one meaningful role, and a row of chips would suggest a permission model the application does not have. The highest-privilege match wins so that a Schichtleiter who also carries operator is not labelled the lesser of the two.
- `signOutOpen: unknown = signal(false)`
- `t: unknown = this.i18n.t`
- `username: unknown = this.auth.username`

Methods:

"Abmelden" sits in a header toolbar next to the language switch on a device operated with work gloves, and an accidental sign-out costs a full Keycloak round trip in the middle of a fault — the one moment nobody has time for it.
- `use(language: UiLanguage): void`

### Dialog

File: `src/app/shared/dialog/dialog.ts`
Selector: `app-dialog`
Standalone: yes
Change detection: `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`

Description: The modal shell every dialog in this application is built from: backdrop, head with a title and a close button, scrolling body, focus trap, Esc. Why not \<dialog\> . The native element gives focus trapping and Esc for free, and it is the right choice in a browser — but the test runner is vitest in jsdom, which does not implement showModal() , so a native dialog would be untestable in the only place this project runs tests. The behaviour is therefore implemented here: Esc closes, Tab cycles inside, the first control takes focus on open and the opener gets it back on close. That is the part users notice; the element is an implementation detail. It was the help dialog's own code until the shop floor needed two more dialogs. Extracting it is what keeps "focus returns to the trigger" a property of every dialog rather than of the one that happened to be written first.

Inputs:
- `open: boolean = false`
- `testId: string = 'dialog'` — What the dialog is called in the DOM, so a test can address one dialog rather than "the dialog". The three parts get \<testId\>-backdrop , \<testId\>-dialog and \<testId\>-close .
- `title: string = ''`

Outputs:
- `closed: void`

Properties:
- `document: unknown = inject(DOCUMENT)`
- `i18n: unknown = inject(I18nService)`
- `opener: HTMLElement | null = null` — Whoever opened the dialog, so focus can be handed back where it came from.
- `panel: unknown = viewChild<ElementRef<HTMLElement>>('panel')`
- `t: unknown = this.i18n.t`
- `` titleId: unknown = `dialog-title-${++sequence}` ``

Methods:
- `close(): void`
- `focusables(): HTMLElement[]`
- `onKeydown(event: KeyboardEvent): void` — Esc closes from anywhere inside the dialog — the shortcut every modal is expected to have.
- `trapTab(event: KeyboardEvent): void` — Keeps Tab inside the dialog. Without this, tabbing walks out of a modal and onto the page behind it, which for a screen reader user means the dialog silently stops being where they are.

What is left here is the content, which is the only part specific to help.

### Landing

File: `src/app/features/landing/landing.ts`
Selector: `app-landing`
Standalone: yes
Change detection: `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`

Description: The logged-out landing page: what this is, why it exists, and how to try it. It is the first screen a recruiter sees and it has about ninety seconds. So it leads with the problem rather than the stack, states the two things that make the answers trustworthy (sourced or labelled, processed in the EU), and puts the demo accounts and three questions that actually retrieve something within reach — a demo whose visitor cannot think of a question shows nothing. It replaces the Phase 1 login page and keeps its route, because postLogoutRedirectUri points at /login : signing out lands here, which is the right place to land.

Properties:
- `auth: unknown = inject(AuthService)`
- `demoPassword: unknown = DEMO_PASSWORD`
- `demoUsers: unknown = DEMO_USERS`
- `i18n: unknown = inject(I18nService)`
- `router: unknown = inject(Router)`
- `signedOut: unknown = signal(false)` — Set when this tab arrived here from a sign-out, so the landing page can confirm it happened.
- `t: unknown = this.i18n.t`

Methods:
- `signIn(username?: string): void` — Starts the redirect to Keycloak on an explicit click rather than on load: an automatic redirect turns any transient Keycloak error into a loop the visitor cannot escape. With a username it is the same redirect carrying login\_hint , so Keycloak prefills the field and the visitor only types the password. It is emphatically not a one-click login: see DECISIONS.txt on why the password grant and a credential-filling login theme were both rejected.

### ProtocolDialog

File: `src/app/shared/protocol/protocol-dialog.ts`
Selector: `app-protocol-dialog`
Standalone: yes
Change detection: `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`

Description: The in-app protocol viewer. Why the document no longer leaves the application. #26 fetched the protocol as a blob through HttpClient — necessary, because a browser-followed anchor carries no Bearer token — and then opened it in a new tab as an object URL. That solved the 401 and left the reader in the browser's raw text viewer: unstyled, outside the application, and on a shop-floor tablet or a kiosk terminal a place that is genuinely hard to get back from. Rendering it here removes the category of problem instead of working around it: nothing navigates, so nothing can navigate without a token, and the synchronous window.open dance with its popup-blocker fallback is simply gone. The request itself is unchanged — the same GET /api/protocols/{id}/document through the same interceptor. The backend was not touched. The download action is the one remaining use of a blob URL in the application, and it is the right one: saving a file is exactly what an object URL is for.

Inputs:
- `machine: string = ''` — The machine the question was asked about — the second half of "which document is this".
- `protocolId: string | null = null` — The protocol to show, or null when the viewer is closed. Setting it starts the fetch.
- `protocolTitle: string = ''` — What the answer called this protocol, so the dialog names what the reader clicked.

Outputs:
- `closed: void`

Properties:
- `api: unknown = inject(MaintenanceApiService)`
- `canDownload: unknown = computed(() => this.file() !== null)` — Whether a download is possible — the bytes are here even when parsing gave up on them.
- `document: unknown = inject(DOCUMENT)`
- `failure: unknown = signal<ApiFailure | null>(null)`
- `file: unknown = signal<{ blob: Blob; filename: string } | null>(null)` — Held so the download saves the ORIGINAL bytes, not a re-encoding of the parsed text.
- `i18n: unknown = inject(I18nService)`
- `loading: unknown = signal(false)`
- `objectUrl: string | null = null`
- `parsed: unknown = signal<ProtocolDocument | null>(null)`
- `t: unknown = this.i18n.t`

Methods:
- `close(): void`
- `download(): void` — Saves the original file. An object URL rather than a link to the API for the same reason the viewer exists: a download the browser performs from an /api/ href is a fresh navigation with no token on it.
- `load(protocolId: string): void`
- `ngOnDestroy(): void`
- `releaseObjectUrl(): void` — An object URL pins its blob in memory until it is revoked, so a technician clicking through six sources would otherwise leave six documents allocated for the life of the tab. At most one download is live at a time, so holding exactly one and releasing it on the next is enough — and it is not released on close, because a download the user started a moment ago may still be reading it.
- `reset(): void`

### Search

File: `src/app/features/search/search.ts`
Selector: `app-search`
Standalone: yes
Change detection: `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`

Description: The search view (US-1/US-2). The two answer modes are rendered as two visually distinct blocks, which is not styling: NFR-2 makes the distinction the anti-hallucination mechanism. A Mode B answer that looked like a Mode A answer would be the failure this application is built to prevent — general advice read as documented plant experience. So Mode B gets its own colour, its own banner and, deliberately, no source area at all rather than an empty one.

Properties:
- `answer: unknown = signal<QueryAnswer | null>(null)`
- `api: unknown = inject(MaintenanceApiService)`
- `asking: unknown = signal(false)`
- `failure: unknown = signal<ApiFailure | null>(null)`
- `i18n: unknown = inject(I18nService)`
- `machineId: unknown = signal('')`
- ``machineLabel: unknown = computed(() => { const machine = this.machines().find((candidate) => candidate.id === this.machineId()); return machine ? `${machine.machineNo} · ${machine.name…`` — What to call the machine in the viewer's head: the picker's own label, not an id.
- `machines: unknown = signal<Machine[]>([])`
- `machinesFailed: unknown = signal(false)`
- `question: unknown = signal('')`
- `segments: unknown = computed<AnswerSegment[]>(() => { const current = this.answer(); return current && current.mode === 'A' ? toSegments(current.answer, current.citations) : []; })` — The answer text split into prose and citation markers. Computed rather than done in the template so the regular expression runs once per answer instead of once per change detection pass.
- `steps: unknown = computed<string[]>(() => { const current = this.answer(); if (!current || current.mode !== 'B') { return []; } return current.answer .split('\n') .map((step) =>…` — Mode B's steps: the backend joins them with newlines, and they render as a numbered list.
- `t: unknown = this.i18n.t`
- `validation: unknown = signal<'question' | 'machine' | null>(null)`
- `viewing: unknown = signal<Citation | null>(null)` — The citation whose protocol the viewer is showing, or null when the viewer is closed.

Methods:
- `ask(): void`
- `openSource(citation: Citation, event?: Event): void` — Opens the protocol behind a citation, in a dialog, inside the application. Why this is a handler and not an href . It was an href , and it did not work: a browser-followed anchor is a fresh navigation that never passes through Angular's interceptor chain, so it carries no Authorization header, and the backend is a stateless JWT resource server with no cookie fallback — every click answered 401. The first fix (#26) fetched the document through HttpClient and opened it in a new tab as an object URL. That was right about the token and wrong about the destination: it dropped the reader into the browser's raw text viewer, out of the application, which on a shop-floor tablet is somewhere hard to come back from. The viewer dialog keeps the document here, and the whole question of what a navigation carries stops applying. All this method does now is name the citation — the dialog owns the fetch, the parsing and the download.
- `similarityPercent(citation: Citation): number` — Percent, rounded — a reader compares 69 % with 56 %, not 0.6896 with 0.5566.

### ThemeToggle

File: `src/app/shared/theme/theme-toggle.ts`
Selector: `app-theme-toggle`
Standalone: yes
Change detection: `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`

Description: The three-state theme control: system, light, dark. Three buttons rather than a two-state switch, because "follow the operating system" is a real choice and not the absence of one — a two-state control silently turns every user into a manual one the first time they touch it, and then a tablet that used to go dark at dusk stops doing it. Modelled on the language switch next to it: a labelled group of buttons with aria-pressed , rather than a menu. With three options a menu costs a click to discover what three icons already show, and on a touchscreen a popover is the harder target.

Properties:
- `choice: unknown = this.theme.choice`
- `i18n: unknown = inject(I18nService)`
- `t: unknown = this.i18n.t`
- `theme: unknown = inject(ThemeService)`

Methods:
- `use(choice: ThemeChoice): void`

### Upload

File: `src/app/features/upload/upload.ts`
Selector: `app-upload`
Standalone: yes
Change detection: `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`

Description: The Schichtleiter's upload view. Write access belongs to one role by decision (DECISIONS.txt: quality, consistency, anti-garbage), and the route is guarded accordingly — but the guard is convenience. The backend refuses the upload for anyone else, which is the check that counts (NFR-3). The view is built around the fact that upload answers 202, not 201 : the protocol exists but is not searchable until a worker has chunked and embedded it. Hiding that behind a success message would teach a Schichtleiter that uploading and being findable are the same event, and the first time indexing failed they would have no idea. So the status list is part of the view, and it shows the failure reason rather than only the failure.

Properties:
- `accepted: unknown = signal(false)`
- `api: unknown = inject(MaintenanceApiService)`
- `errorCode: unknown = signal('')`
- `failure: unknown = signal<ApiFailure | null>(null)`
- `file: unknown = signal<File | null>(null)`
- `i18n: unknown = inject(I18nService)`
- `language: unknown = signal<'de' | 'en'>('de')`
- `machineNo: unknown = signal('')`
- `machines: unknown = signal<Machine[]>([])`
- `refreshing: unknown = signal(false)`
- `submitting: unknown = signal(false)`
- `t: unknown = this.i18n.t`
- `title: unknown = signal('')`
- `type: unknown = signal<'STOERUNG' | 'WARTUNG'>('STOERUNG')`
- `uploads: unknown = signal<UploadStatus[]>([])`

Methods:
- `pickFile(event: Event): void`
- `refresh(): void` — Reloads the status list on demand. Manual rather than polled. Indexing takes seconds, a poll would run for the whole time the tab is open, and every one of those requests costs a database round trip to answer "still the same". A button the user presses when they care is smaller, cheaper and easier to reason about than a timer somebody has to remember to clear.
- `shortDate(iso: string): string` — Date only: the exact second an upload happened has never been the question.
- `statusLabel(status: UploadStatus): string`
- `submit(): void`

## Services / Injectables

### AuthService

File: `src/app/core/auth/auth.service.ts`
providedIn: `root`

Description: Wraps angular-oauth2-oidc so components never touch the OIDC library directly. Roles are read from the access token , not the ID token: Keycloak puts realm roles in realm\_access.roles there. They drive what the UI shows — the backend enforces the same roles server-side, because hiding a button is not a security control (NFR-3).

Properties:
- `authState: unknown = signal(0)` — Bumped after every login/logout so the derived signals recompute.
- `configService: unknown = inject(ConfigService)`
- `isAuthenticated: unknown = computed(() => { this.authState(); return this.oauth.hasValidAccessToken(); })`
- `oauth: unknown = inject(OAuthService)`
- `realmRoles: unknown = computed(() => { this.authState(); return this.claims()?.realm_access?.roles ?? []; })`
- `username: unknown = computed(() => { this.authState(); return this.claims()?.preferred_username ?? ''; })`

Methods:
- `claims(): AccessTokenClaims | null` — Decodes the access token payload; returns null when there is no valid token.
- `consumeSignedOutNotice(): boolean` — Whether this tab has just signed out, clearing the flag as it reports it. Read-and-clear rather than read: the notice is about the sign-out that just happened, and one that reappeared on every later visit to the landing page would stop meaning anything.
- `init(): Promise<void>` — Configures the client, fetches the discovery document and completes a redirect that is coming back from Keycloak. Runs once during application startup.
- `login(loginHint?: string): void` — Sends the browser to Keycloak's login page. loginHint is passed as the standard login\_hint authorization request parameter, which Keycloak uses to prefill the username field. It is a hint on the normal Auth Code + PKCE request and nothing more: the visitor still authenticates at Keycloak, and the password never passes through this application. The demo buttons on the landing page are its only caller.
- `logout(): void`
- `rememberSignOut(): void`

### ConfigService

File: `src/app/core/config/config.service.ts`
providedIn: `root`

Description: Loads RuntimeConfig from /config.json once, during startup. A missing or malformed file is not an error: the values compiled into environment.ts are used instead. That keeps the image runnable on its own — a deployment that forgets the bind mount serves the built-in defaults rather than a blank page.

Properties:
- `current: RuntimeConfig = this.fallback`
- `fallback: RuntimeConfig = { keycloakIssuer: environment.keycloakIssuer, keycloakClientId: environment.keycloakClientId, apiBaseUrl: environment.apiBaseUrl, }`

Methods:
- `load(): Promise<void>` — Fetched with fetch rather than HttpClient on purpose: this runs before the first route renders, and the interceptor chain HttpClient carries is set up to attach an access token that does not exist yet.

### I18nService

File: `src/app/core/i18n/i18n.service.ts`
providedIn: `root`

Description: The DE/EN switch, as a runtime dictionary rather than Angular's build-time i18n. Angular's $localize produces one bundle per locale, which means two builds, two images and a routing or host decision to pick between them. For two languages and one small application that is a deployment problem bought to solve a string problem — and it would make the language a property of the URL rather than of the person, so switching would reload the page and lose the answer on screen. A signal holding one of two typed objects switches instantly and ships one bundle. The UI language is not the answer language. The backend pins every answer to the language of the question (ADR-002's language rule), and nothing is translated anywhere in this system by decision. So a German answer stays German with the interface in English: this service changes labels, never content. The rendered answer carries its own lang attribute for exactly that reason.

Properties:
- `current: unknown = signal<UiLanguage>(initialLanguage())`
- `language: unknown = this.current.asReadonly()` — The active language, for lang attributes and for the switch's own state.
- `t: unknown = computed<Dictionary>(() => DICTIONARIES[this.current()])` — The active dictionary. Components read t().search.submit and re-render on a switch.

Methods:
- `toggle(): void`
- `use(language: UiLanguage): void`

### MaintenanceApiService

File: `src/app/core/api/maintenance-api.service.ts`
providedIn: `root`

Description: The five calls this application makes to its own backend. One service rather than one per feature: the API is small, and splitting it would mean three files that each inject the same base URL to make one request. The access token is attached by angular-oauth2-oidc 's resource-server interceptor, configured once in app.config.ts , so nothing here touches a header.

Properties:
- `apiBaseUrl: unknown = inject(ConfigService).config.apiBaseUrl`
- `http: unknown = inject(HttpClient)`

Methods:
- `ask(question: string, machineId: string): Observable<QueryAnswer>` — Asks a question about one machine. Search is scoped to exactly one machine by decision, so machineId is required rather than optional-with-a-default: a question answered from another machine's protocols would look like a better feature and be a worse answer.
- `getDocument(protocolId: string): Observable<HttpResponse<Blob>>` — Fetches a protocol's original document. Through HttpClient, and that is the whole point. This used to be a method returning the URL for an \<a href\> , and it did not work: a browser-followed anchor is a fresh navigation that never passes through Angular's interceptor chain, so it carries no Authorization header. The backend is a stateless JWT resource server with no session and no cookie fallback ( SecurityConfig ), so every such click answered 401. Returning a URL at all is what invited the mistake, so no method here returns one. observe: 'response' rather than the body alone because the response headers are the useful half: Content-Type decides whether the browser renders the document or downloads it, and Content-Disposition carries the readable filename the backend built.
- `machines(): Observable<Machine[]>` — The machines a question can be asked about.
- `myUploads(): Observable<UploadStatus[]>` — The caller's own uploads and what became of them. Schichtleiter only, server-side.
- `upload(form: FormData): Observable<UploadAccepted>` — Uploads a protocol document. Answers 202: stored, not yet searchable.

### ThemeService

File: `src/app/core/theme/theme.service.ts`
providedIn: `root`

Description: The theme, as a three-state choice with the operating system as the default. Why the operating system is resolved here rather than by a media query. The dark palette used to live in @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) . A manual override on top of that needs the dark values to apply under two conditions at once — the media query and an attribute — and CSS has no way to share one declaration block between them, so the values would exist twice and drift apart the first time one of them was edited. Resolving the preference in TypeScript and writing a single data-theme attribute keeps the dark palette in exactly one place in the stylesheet, which is the property that matters: the two themes cannot disagree about a colour nobody remembered to change in both. The cost is that the theme now depends on JavaScript. For an application that is a single-page Angular bundle behind a login redirect, that dependency already existed.

Properties:
- `choice: unknown = this.choiceSignal.asReadonly()`
- `choiceSignal: unknown = signal<ThemeChoice>(storedChoice())`
- `document: unknown = inject(DOCUMENT)`
- `resolved: unknown = computed<ResolvedTheme>(() => { const choice = this.choiceSignal(); if (choice !== 'system') { return choice; } return this.systemDark() ? 'dark' : 'light'; })`
- `systemDark: unknown = signal(this.matchesDark())` — Tracked separately so a change of the OS setting repaints a system user without a reload.

Methods:
- `apply(theme: ResolvedTheme): void`
- `matchesDark(): boolean`
- `use(choice: ThemeChoice): void`
- `watchSystem(): void`

## Guards

### authGuard

File: `src/app/core/auth/auth.guard.ts`

Description: Blocks routes for callers without a valid access token and sends them to /login. This is convenience, not security: every protected resource is enforced again by the backend resource server, which is the only place an authorization decision actually counts (NFR-3).

## Interfaces

### AccessTokenClaims

File: `src/app/core/auth/auth.service.ts`

Description: Shape of the Keycloak access token claims this application reads.

Properties:
- `preferred_username?: string`
- `realm_access?: { roles?: string[] }`

### AnswerSegment

File: `src/app/features/search/search.ts`

Description: One piece of the answer text: either prose, or a citation marker that links to its source. The answer arrives with its \[P1\] markers already in the text and its claims already validated against what was retrieved. Splitting it here is presentation only — the markers become links. Nothing is re-parsed, reordered or filtered: the backend decided what the answer says, and a client that second-guessed it would be a second, weaker citation check in the place least able to make one.

Properties:
- `citation?: Citation` — For a marker: the citation it points at, when the label is one of the answer's sources.
- `kind: "text" | "marker"`
- `value: string`

### Citation

File: `src/app/core/api/api.types.ts`

Description: A cited protocol. Mode A only; Mode B returns an empty list.

Properties:
- `errorCode: string | null`
- `incidentDate: string | null`
- `label: string`
- `protocolId: string`
- `similarity: number` — Cosine similarity, 0..1. Shown so the demo can say why this is Mode A and the next is Mode B.
- `title: string`

### Claim

File: `src/app/core/api/api.types.ts`

Description: One statement and the label of the source it came from. Mode A only.

Properties:
- `source: string` — Matches a Citation.label — P1 , P2 , …
- `text: string`

### DemoExample

File: `src/app/core/i18n/dictionary.ts`

Description: One of the demo questions offered on the landing page and in the help dialog. Each is tied to a seeded demo case, so the three of them together show the three behaviours worth showing: several sources for one fault, a German question answered from an English protocol, and the deliberate gap that produces a Mode B answer.

Properties:
- `machine: string` — The machine to pick before asking — the query is filtered by machine, so this is not decoration.
- `question: string`
- `shows: string` — What the reader should watch for in the answer.

- `type: string`

### MetaRow

File: `src/app/shared/protocol/protocol-document.ts`

Properties:
- `label: string`
- `value: string`

### ProtocolDocument

File: `src/app/shared/protocol/protocol-document.ts`

Description: A protocol as the viewer will render it. kind is the honest half: 'parsed' means the structure below was recognised, 'raw' means it was not and the viewer must fall back to the file as it stands. The corpus ships a documented quality mix (90 well-written, 45 terse, 15 messy) and one uploaded protocol already has no banner, no header block and no title at all — so "the parser did not recognise this" is a normal outcome to be rendered, not an error to be reported.

Properties:
- `kind: "parsed" | "raw"`
- `raw: string`
- `segments: {}`

### QueryAnswer

File: `src/app/core/api/api.types.ts`

Description: The answer, from POST /api/query . answer already carries its inline \[P1\] markers and its claims are already validated against what was retrieved. The client renders it; it does not re-parse, reorder or second-guess it.

Properties:
- `answer: string`
- `citations: {}`
- `claims: {}`
- `language: string` — The language the backend pinned the answer to — independent of the UI language.
- `mode: AnswerMode`

### RuntimeConfig

File: `src/app/core/config/runtime-config.ts`

Description: Configuration the application reads at runtime rather than at build time. The container image is built once by CI and deployed to every environment, so it cannot contain a hostname. The deployment supplies /config.json instead — a bind mount in production, a static file under public/ in development — and the values compiled into environment.ts are the fallback when that file is missing or unreadable.

Properties:
- `apiBaseUrl: string` — Backend base URL. Same-origin in every environment, so a relative path.
- `keycloakClientId: string` — Public client id from the versioned realm export.
- `keycloakIssuer: string` — Keycloak realm base URL — the OIDC issuer.

### UploadAccepted

File: `src/app/core/api/api.types.ts`

Description: What POST /api/protocols answers with its 202.

Properties:
- `id: string`
- `message: string`
- `status: string`

### UploadStatus

File: `src/app/core/api/api.types.ts`

Description: One of the caller's uploads, from GET /api/protocols/mine .

Properties:
- `createdAt: string`
- `failureReason: string | null` — Why it failed; null unless FAILED.
- `id: string`
- `indexedAt: string | null`
- `machineNo: string`
- `status: "RECEIVED" | "INDEXED" | "FAILED"`
- `title: string`

## Public functions

- `buildAuthConfig(config: RuntimeConfig): AuthConfig` — Builds the OIDC client configuration for the Keycloak realm maintenance (ADR-003). A function rather than a constant because the issuer is only known once /config.json has been read — the image is environment-agnostic, so nothing about the deployment can be decided at module-evaluation time. Authorization Code Flow with PKCE: the browser is a public client that cannot keep a secret, so PKCE replaces the client secret.
  Defined in `src/app/core/auth/auth.config.ts`
- `classify(error): ApiFailure` — Maps a failed request to the message the user should read. The NFR-7 guards reach the surface here, and they mean different things to a person: 429 is "you, in a moment", a spent daily budget is "everyone, tomorrow", and an unreachable provider is "try again shortly". One text for all three would make a rate limit look like an outage. The backend sends both budget exhaustion and provider trouble as 503 and distinguishes them with a reason code in the body. The code is read rather than the message, so rewording the English sentence on the server does not silently change what the German UI says.
  Defined in `src/app/core/api/maintenance-api.service.ts`
- `filenameOf(contentDisposition): string` — The readable filename the backend put in Content-Disposition , for the download action.
  Defined in `src/app/shared/protocol/protocol-document.ts`
- `initialLanguage(): UiLanguage` — A remembered choice wins; otherwise the browser decides. German is the fallback rather than English because the plant, the corpus and the demo users are German — the setting this models is a German shop floor, and a visitor whose browser says nothing useful is better served by the language the protocols are written in.
  Defined in `src/app/core/i18n/i18n.service.ts`
- `parseProtocol(text: string): ProtocolDocument` — Parses a protocol file into typed segments, and never throws. The structure is stable across the corpus but not guaranteed: it is plain text written by people, and the messy end of the quality mix omits whichever part it feels like. So every step is optional. A file with only sections parses; a file with only a header block parses; a file that matches nothing at all comes back as 'raw' and the viewer shows it preformatted. What must never happen is a blank dialog — the reader clicked a citation and is entitled to the evidence behind it, in whatever shape it exists.
  Defined in `src/app/shared/protocol/protocol-document.ts`
- `readMeta(lines, from: number): MetaRow[]` — The run of Key: Value lines starting at from , which ends at the first line that is not one.
  Defined in `src/app/shared/protocol/protocol-document.ts`
- `readSections(lines, from: number): ProtocolSegment[]` — Everything from from on, grouped under the section labels it contains. Text appearing before the first label is kept under an empty heading rather than dropped: an unlabelled paragraph is still what the technician wrote, and losing it would make the viewer a less complete record than the file.
  Defined in `src/app/shared/protocol/protocol-document.ts`
- `reasonOf(error: HttpErrorResponse): string | null` — The body is JSON in practice and untyped in principle; a missing code is simply not a match.
  Defined in `src/app/core/api/maintenance-api.service.ts`
- `roleGuard(...allowed): CanActivateFn` — Keeps a route out of the hands of roles that have no business on it. Like authGuard, this is convenience and not security: the upload endpoint refuses anyone but a Schichtleiter server-side, which is the only place the decision counts (NFR-3). What this buys is that an operator following a bookmarked /upload link gets the search view rather than a form that produces a 403 after they have chosen a file.
  Defined in `src/app/core/auth/role.guard.ts`
- `skipBanner(lines): number` — Steps over the banner line and its ===== rule, if the file has them.
  Defined in `src/app/shared/protocol/protocol-document.ts`
- `skipBlank(lines, from: number): number`
  Defined in `src/app/shared/protocol/protocol-document.ts`
- `storedChoice(): ThemeChoice` — The stored override, or system when there is none. Anything unrecognised counts as no override rather than as an error: the key is in localStorage where a user or an old build could have left anything, and the worst outcome of a bad value should be the default theme.
  Defined in `src/app/core/theme/theme.service.ts`
- `toSegments(answer: string, citations): AnswerSegment[]` — Splits an answer into prose and \[Pn\] markers. A marker whose label is not among the citations is left as plain text rather than dropped or linked: the backend already removed every claim citing a source it did not retrieve, so if one still appears here it belongs to prose and inventing a link for it would be the client asserting something the server did not.
  Defined in `src/app/features/search/search.ts`

## Public type aliases

- `type AnswerMode = "A" | "B"` — NFR-2's two answer modes.
- `type ApiFailure = "rateLimited" | "budgetExhausted" | "unavailable" | "forbidden" | "notFound" | "generic"` — The statuses the UI has a specific sentence for. Everything else collapses to a generic message, deliberately: inventing a distinct wording per status code produces a wall of text nobody maintains, and the three below are the ones a user can actually act on — wait a moment, come back tomorrow, or ask someone for a role.
- `type KnownRole = typeof KNOWN_ROLES['number']`
- `type ProtocolSegment = literal type | literal type | literal type` — One piece of a parsed protocol. Typed segments, exactly like the answer renderer's: the template switches on kind and binds text, so there is no path from a protocol file into innerHTML . The corpus is synthetic today and a Schichtleiter can upload arbitrary text tomorrow, which makes this the same rule and not merely the same style.
- `type ResolvedTheme = "light" | "dark"` — What is actually on screen once system has been resolved against the operating system.
- `type ThemeChoice = "light" | "dark" | "system"` — What the user chose, which is not the same as what is painted. system is a real third state and not the absence of a choice: someone who has deliberately gone back to following the operating system has expressed a preference, and it has to survive a reload the same way the other two do.
- `type UiLanguage = "de" | "en"` — The two languages the interface is offered in (DECISIONS.txt: bilingual DE/EN).

- `environment: object = { production: true, /** Keycloak realm base URL — the OIDC issuer (ADR-003). */ keycloakIssuer: 'https://auth.smartsupply.com.de/realms/maintenance', /** Public…` — Production defaults, compiled into the bundle. These are only the fallback. The deployment supplies /config.json , which ConfigService merges over them at startup, so the same image can be pointed at a different Keycloak without a rebuild. They are kept accurate anyway: an image that loses its bind mount should still reach the real deployment rather than a placeholder host.

- `SECTION_LINE: unknown = /^(.{1,40}):[ \t]*$/` — A section label alone on its line — the value-less form is what separates it from a meta row.

- `sequence: number = 0` — Makes each instance's title element addressable by aria-labelledby without a collision.
  Defined in `src/app/shared/dialog/dialog.ts`
- `SIGNED_OUT_KEY: string = 'maintenance-assistant.signed-out'` — Marks that this tab signed out deliberately, so the landing page can say so. sessionStorage rather than a query parameter on the redirect: postLogoutRedirectUri is matched against the URIs registered in the realm, and decorating it would risk a Keycloak change this project has decided not to need. It is also the right lifetime — the notice belongs to the tab that signed out, not to every tab on the machine. logOut() clears only its own keys, so this one survives the round trip through Keycloak.
  Defined in `src/app/core/auth/auth.service.ts`
- `STORAGE_KEY: string = 'maintenance-assistant.language'` — Where the choice is remembered between visits.
  Defined in `src/app/core/i18n/i18n.service.ts`
- `THEME_STORAGE_KEY: string = 'ma-theme'` — Where the choice is remembered. Shared with public/theme-init.js , which reads the same key before Angular exists — change one and the other stops agreeing.
  Defined in `src/app/core/theme/theme.service.ts`
